name: Sprint/HIIT for growth hormone

card.summary: Sprints and HIIT do raise growth hormone briefly, but no trial shows they add height.
card.note: Exercise-induced GH rises are temporary; no study links them to final height.

quick.overview:
Some teens do sprints or interval training because intense exercise raises growth hormone, which is involved in childhood growth.

The exercise-GH link is documented, but no published trial has tested whether such workouts change adult height.
quick.mechanism: Vigorous exercise is a recognised stimulus of GH pulses, and GH acts on growth cartilage directly and through IGF-1. Believers extend this to a height effect; reference sources do not report that extension.
quick.risks: Sprint and interval training carry the usual risks of high-intensity exercise such as muscle and tendon strain. Adult height is described as largely genetic, with nutrition and health as the main modifiable factors.

lead: Sprint or high-intensity interval training (HIIT) for growth hormone is a height-related practice in which teenagers do all-out sprints or interval workouts in the belief that the resulting surge in growth hormone (GH) will help them grow taller or look more developed. It rests on the fact that vigorous exercise is a recognised stimulus of GH secretion, and GH is the hormone best known for its role in childhood growth.[1]

Wikipedia describes increased childhood height as GH's most widely known effect, working both directly on cartilage cells and through IGF-1 made mainly in the liver, and notes that young adolescents secrete roughly 700 micrograms a day versus about 400 in healthy adults.[1] HIIT itself alternates short, intense efforts with brief recoveries, and the same encyclopedia entry reports that in adolescents it can increase muscle mass, especially in the mid-to-late teens, and can reduce body fat in youth with obesity.[3] For appearance, that gives the practice a second payoff alongside the height hope: a leaner, more muscular build.

Small studies of sprint exercise confirm that GH rises after a single maximal effort and stays elevated for one to two hours, and that the rise is larger for 30-second sprints than for 6-second ones.[5] Adult height is described as largely heritable, with nutrition and health in childhood the main environmental factors, and no published trial has tested sprint or HIIT training as a way to change final height in healthy adolescents.[2]

chain: Sprints and intervals stimulate GH release
GH and IGF-1 support growth in the growing years
Taller frame (as practitioners hope), plus leaner, more muscular build
angle.text: Practitioners use sprints and interval circuits to trigger natural GH pulses while growth plates are still open. Separately, HIIT is documented to build fitness and, in teens, muscle and lower body fat, which changes how the body looks.

infobox: Growth hormone, IGF-1, also testosterone in sprint studies[1][5]

paras: Practitioners describe short, maximal-effort sprints, hill sprints or interval circuits performed several times a week, sometimes combined with sleep and nutrition routines, with the stated aim of maximising natural GH release during the years when growth is still possible.

HIIT is a training format with a warm-up, intense intervals separated by easier recovery, and a cool-down. Wikipedia reports sessions typically run under 30 minutes, intervals usually last 20 to 45 seconds, and a common ratio is about 2:1 work to rest, though there is no single formula.[3] Sprint interval training (SIT) is a variant using supramaximal all-out efforts in shorter bursts with lower total volume and longer recovery.[3]

sections.h: How people use it for their looks
paras: For height, teenagers and parents who follow height-growth forums add sprinting to routines alongside sleep, nutrition and stretching, reasoning that a GH pulse during puberty can only help. For physique, interval work is used as a time-efficient way to lose fat and build athletic conditioning; a T Nation thread asks whether high-intensity training helps fat loss, reflecting the same interest in lean, defined appearance.[6]
Sprint sessions are commonly done on a track, hill, bike or treadmill. Because the GH response depends on the effort, practitioners aim for truly maximal bursts rather than steady jogging.[5]

The method is often traced to Peter Coe, who in the 1970s had his son Sebastian Coe repeat fast 200 metre runs with short recoveries.[3] In 1996 Izumi Tabata of Ritsumeikan University and colleagues studied Olympic speed skaters on 20 seconds of very hard effort followed by 10 seconds of rest repeated for 8 cycles; over 6 weeks it matched the aerobic gains of a steady-state group while adding anaerobic capacity.[3] Martin Gibala of McMaster University popularised a 60-seconds-hard, 75-seconds-easy cycling format in 2010, and Vollaard later proposed a protocol of two 20-second all-out sprints.[3]

Doping and sports-medicine history adds context: athletes have used synthetic GH since at least 1982, and recombinant GH was FDA-approved in 1985, which is part of why GH has become a cultural shorthand for growth and physique.[1]

GH is released in pulses. Wikipedia lists sleep, vigorous exercise, fasting, sex hormones in puberty and ghrelin among stimulators, describes the largest daily peak as occurring about an hour after sleep onset, and notes that sleep deprivation suppresses release.[1] In children, GH deficiency causes growth failure and short stature, which underlies the idea that more GH could mean more height; recombinant GH is used for childhood growth disorders and other conditions under medical supervision.[1]

Twin studies cited by Wikipedia estimate that 60 to 80 percent of height variation within a population is heritable, and growth reaches zero on average around 15 to 16 in females and 18 to 19 in males.[2] Epiphyseal (growth) plates fuse as early as 12 in girls and 14 in boys, most commonly at 14 to 15 and 15 to 17 respectively, and rising estrogen during puberty reduces growth-plate cartilage activity until growth stops.[4] Chronic malnutrition during childhood is associated with reduced adult height.[2]

In a within-subject study of nine men, a single 30-second maximal cycle sprint produced a peak mean GH more than 450 percent higher than a 6-second sprint and kept GH elevated for 90 to 120 minutes, compared with about 60 minutes after the shorter sprint; there was large variation between individuals, and GH did not rise in a no-exercise control trial.[5]

In 27 non-obese men aged 18 to 32, GH rose after a 30-second sprint and age was a significant negative predictor of the response, while sprint performance and BMI were not.[5] Two small studies of elite junior handball players aged 17 to 25 found that treadmill sprint-interval sessions raised GH, IGFBP-3, testosterone and the inflammatory marker IL-6, and that a decreasing-distance session produced a larger GH response than an increasing-distance one.[5] The studies measured hormone levels after a session, not height.

Wikipedia reports HIIT modestly reduces subcutaneous fat in healthy people and more in overweight people, and that in teens 8 to 12 weeks of HIIT combined with resistance training reduced waist size and body fat percentage in a 2021 review covering ages 10 to 19.[3] HIIT programmes of a month or more improved cardiovascular fitness in adolescents, and it may be less effective than longer sessions for building muscle or bone mass.[3]

The American College of Sports Medicine recommends consulting a doctor before starting, especially with a history of coronary heart disease, and starting at lower intensity. High-intensity exercise can cause rapid blood pressure spikes, injury risk rises with fatigue and overtraining, and knees, shoulders and ankles are the most commonly injured areas in cited research.[3] Growth-plate injuries such as Salter-Harris fractures can interfere with growth, and Osgood-Schlatter disease involves stress on the tibial growth plate.[4]

No studies found on sprint or HIIT training and final height in adolescents. Related research measures the acute hormone response: GH rises temporarily after maximal sprints in adults and elite junior athletes, with a larger rise after 30-second than after 6-second efforts.[5]

timeline.event: Peter Coe sets Sebastian Coe repeated fast 200 m runs with short recoveries, an early form of interval training.[3]
Athletes' use of synthetic GH is first described in Dan Duchaine's Underground Steroid Handbook.[1]
Recombinant human GH approved by the FDA.[1]
Izumi Tabata and colleagues publish the 20-seconds-on, 10-seconds-off interval protocol in Olympic speed skaters.[3]
Stokes and colleagues report the time course of GH after 6-second and 30-second cycle sprints.[5]
Martin Gibala's McMaster group popularises a low-volume cycling interval format.[3]
A review of adolescents aged 10 to 19 finds HIIT plus resistance training reduced waist size and body fat.[3]

lore.intro: In height-focused forum discussion, sprinting and HIIT are often listed among free ways to support growth during puberty, and in physique discussion HIIT is a staple for fat loss.[6]

claims.claim: Sprinting spikes GH, so it makes teens taller
claims.believers: Proponents point to the well-known exercise-induced GH rise and argue that more GH pulses during puberty should translate to extra growth.
claims.experts: Reference sources confirm that vigorous exercise stimulates GH secretion but do not report that this changes final height; heritability of 60 to 80 percent and nutrition are the factors described, and no trial has tested the question.[1][2]

claims.claim: Sprints must be all-out to trigger GH
claims.believers: Practitioners say only maximal efforts produce the pulse and favour short all-out bursts over steady cardio.
claims.experts: Cycle-sprint studies found GH peaks were much larger after a 30-second than a 6-second maximal sprint, and individual responses varied widely.[5]

claims.claim: HIIT in the teens builds a leaner, more athletic physique
claims.believers: Practitioners present interval work as a time-efficient way to lose fat and gain athletic conditioning.
claims.experts: Reviews summarised by Wikipedia report reduced body fat and increased muscle mass in adolescents on HIIT programmes, with resistance training added.[3]

claims.claim: Young people get a bigger GH boost from sprinting than older people
claims.believers: Teen height forums assume the pubertal GH surge makes exercise especially potent.
claims.experts: A study of 27 men aged 18 to 32 found age negatively predicted the GH response to a sprint; adolescents were not studied there.[5][1]

claims.claim: Poor sleep cancels the benefit of training for growth
claims.believers: Practitioners pair sprints with sleep routines because the largest daily GH pulse comes soon after sleep onset.
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the main GH peak about an hour after sleep begins and notes sleep deprivation suppresses GH release; the effect on height has not been tested with exercise.[1]

claims.claim: Intense training stunts growth by damaging growth plates
claims.believers: Some parents and forum posters fear heavy training closes plates early.
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes growth-plate fractures can interfere with growth and that plates fuse at typical ages set by hormones; no published study cited there links routine training to early plate closure.[4]
